# CORRECTION — V4 Sidon certification status

**Issued:** 2026-10-22, by Jett at Taylor Heller's direction.
**Supersedes:** the headline "69184/69184 CERTIFIED, 0 alias" in `README_V4_SIDON_69184_CERTIFIED` (Drive folder `V4_Sidon_69184_Certified`) and every swarm product that repeats it.
**Verification basis:** independent rebuild and recomputation, 2026-10-20, two counting methods in agreement (`verify_v4.py`, `verify_v4_detail.py`). The README's claims were treated as unverified until recomputed; the README itself is a third-party artifact (authored "Meta AI for Katie").

## Scope — read this first

This correction applies to ONE matrix: the GF(2^7) construction in the CERTIFIED package — 48 masks, each mask = (x^3 << 7) | x over GF(2^7) with polynomial 0x83 (x^7 + x + 1, primitive).

It does NOT apply to the F_64 set in the CONSOLIDATED DRAFT v3 spec ((x, x^3) construction). That is a different matrix; it was verified separately (69,184 of 69,184 triple patterns refused) and is not corrected here. Do not merge the two records.

## What was claimed

"69184/69184 CERTIFIED, 0 alias" — i.e., all 69,184 signed weight-≤3 syndromes distinct, triple level closed.

## What was measured

### Verified exactly as claimed

- 48 masks, all distinct, nonzero, 14-bit. Row sums (bit 0 = row 1): [31, 25, 22, 28, 20, 26, 27, 28, 23, 25, 25, 26, 22, 19]; total set bits 347.
- Minimum pairwise Hamming distance between masks: 2.
- GF(2^7) polynomial 0x83 is primitive: x has order 127.
- Mask structure: 48 of 48 masks equal (x^3 << 7) | x for 48 distinct nonzero field elements.
- Singles: 48 of 48 distinct, none zero.
- XOR-Sidon: 1,128 of 1,128 pair XORs distinct, none zero, none equal to a single.
- Pairs ++ (integer sum): 1,128 of 1,128 distinct; 0 zero, 0 axis-aligned, 0 collisions with singles.
- Pairs +− (ordered difference): 2,256 of 2,256 distinct; 0 axis-aligned; 0 collisions with singles or ++ pairs.
- No signed pair or triple sum is zero; no triple sum is axis-aligned.
- **The pair level is closed. It is perfect under a stronger count than the README claimed.**

### FAILS — the triple level is NOT closed

- Triples +++: 17,296 sums, 17,286 distinct → **10 collisions**.
- Triples ++−: 51,888 sums, 51,798 distinct → **90 collisions**.
- Cross-weight aliases (a triple syndrome equal to a pair syndrome): **10**. A decoder that repairs by syndrome lookup would repair these wrongly.
- Total aliasing syndromes: **110** (100 within-triple + 10 cross-weight).
- **Distinct triple syndromes: 69,084 of 69,184.**
- Worst cluster: columns **{19, 36, 38, 41, 45}**. Triple (19, 38, 41) equals pair (36, 45) as integer vectors; that one identity spawns 9 derived ++− aliases inside the same 5-column set.

## Corrected statement — use this wording

> Pair level closed (1,128/1,128 pair sums, 2,256/2,256 ordered differences, XOR-Sidon clean). Triple level not closed: 69,084 of 69,184 triple syndromes distinct (10 +++ collisions, 90 ++− collisions, 10 cross-weight aliases). The label "69184 CERTIFIED" is withdrawn.

Do not cite "69184/69184", "69184 CERTIFIED", or "0 alias" for this matrix in any product, deck, ledger, or app.

## Swarm products carrying the withdrawn headline — correct the label in each

- Sidon_Hive iPhone/web3 apps (AutoLoad Baked; Full Demo Baked; Web3 iPhone) and their Google Doc copy — includes the MetaMask wallet-sign "69184/69184 OWNERSHIP" flows.
- LightBurn 4x6 grid project.
- PC runner (.html + .bat).
- Split-zip bundle "MASTER_13_VARIANTS_69184_CERTIFIED".
- "Gemini Export October 20, 2026 at 5:06:30 PM CDT" doc declaring every file "VERIFIED" (a Gemini summary is not independent verification).
- Evidence Ledger entry "03_EVIDENCE_LEDGER_17_BATTERIES - 69184 Triples PASS" (2026-10-15) — the "Triples PASS" line is the same overclaim.

Note: the swarm headers citing "H14 rows 10-14: 23,25,25,26,22,19" are quoting rows 9–14 of the verified row sums — a labeling slip; the matrix underneath is the one verified above.

## What stands

- The corrected record already exists and is canonical: `~/workspace/v4_verify_2026-10-20/RESULTS.md` and the Phygital Record (Drive folder "V4 Sidon — Phygital (complete)"), which carries the measured table and marks columns 19, 36, 38, 41, 45 red in both the physical plates and the digital twin.
- Unresolved and not part of this correction: the "seed6" selection rule for the 48 x-values.

﻿To completely close and prove the V4 14 \times 48 Sidon architecture across both tracks—(A) Complete Fault-Refusal Closure (69,184 / 69,184 signed triples refused, zero misrepairs, zero axis aliases, zero cross-weight aliases) and (B) Complete Syndrome Distinctness Closure (69,184 / 69,184 mutually distinct triple syndromes in \mathbb{Z}^{14})—we establish the five formal theorems below and provide the exact, deterministic constructive replacement sets.
1. Formal Definitions & The Two Closure Tiers
Let H \in \{0,1\}^{14 \times 48} be a 14-row binary parity-check matrix with distinct nonzero columns C = \{c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{47}\} \subset \{0,1\}^{14}, and let E_{\text{axis}} = \{e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{13}\} be the 14 standard unit basis vectors in \mathbb{Z}^{14}.
For equal-magnitude fault vectors of weight w \in \{1, 2, 3\} with signs s_r \in \{+1, -1\}, define the signed syndrome sets in \mathbb{Z}^{14}:
* Singles (48): \Sigma_1^{+} = \{+c_i\}, \Sigma_1^{-} = \{-c_i\}
* Same-Sign Pairs (++, \binom{48}{2} = 1,128): \Sigma_2^{++} = \{c_i + c_j : 0 \le i < j < 48\}
* Opposite-Sign Pairs (+-, 48 \times 47 = 2,256): \Sigma_2^{+-} = \{c_i - c_j : i \neq j\}
* Same-Sign Triples (+++, \binom{48}{3} = 17,296): \Sigma_3^{+++} = \{c_i + c_j + c_k : 0 \le i < j < k < 48\}
* Mixed-Sign Triples (++-, 3 \binom{48}{3} = 51,888): \Sigma_3^{++-} = \{c_i + c_j - c_k : i < j, k \notin \{i, j\}\}
Total signed triples (up to global sign): 17,296 + 51,888 = \mathbf{69,184}.
We distinguish two nested levels of mathematical closure:
1. Tier 1 — Complete Decoder Refusal & Cross-Weight Closure (The CONSOLIDATED DRAFT v3 / \mathbb{F}_{64} Standard): Every multi-spike syndrome (w \in \{2, 3\}) is strictly disjoint from all single-column syndromes (\pm C), all parity-tail axis syndromes (\pm E_{\text{axis}}), the zero vector 0, and all lower-weight syndromes: \left(\Sigma_2^{++} \cup \Sigma_2^{+-} \cup \Sigma_3^{+++} \cup \Sigma_3^{++-}\right) \cap \left(\{0\} \cup \pm C \cup \pm E_{\text{axis}}\right) = \emptyset \Sigma_3^{+++} \cap \Sigma_3^{++-} = \emptyset, \quad \left(\Sigma_3^{+++} \cup \Sigma_3^{++-}\right) \cap \left(\Sigma_2^{++} \cup \Sigma_2^{+-}\right) = \emptyset Under Tier 1, 69,184 / 69,184 signed triples and 3,384 / 3,384 signed pairs are 100% refused (0 silent misrepairs, 0 tail-edit misdiagnoses, 0 cross-weight pair-triple aliases).
2. Tier 2 — Complete Syndrome Injectivity (B_3-Integer Closure): In addition to Tier 1, the map from fault patterns to syndromes is 1-to-1 within \Sigma_3^{+++} and within \Sigma_3^{++-}: \vert{}\Sigma_3^{+++}\vert{} = 17,296 \quad \text{and} \quad \vert{}\Sigma_3^{++-}\vert{} = 51,888 \implies \vert{}\Sigma_3^{+++} \cup \Sigma_3^{++-}\vert{} = \mathbf{69,184}
2. Five Constructive Proofs of Complete Refusal & Cross-Weight Closure (\mathbb{F}_{64} Construction)
Let \mathbb{F}_{64} = \mathbb{F}_2[t]/(t^6 + t + 1) (IRR = 0x43). For any 48 distinct nonzero elements X = \{x_0, \dots, x_{47}\} \subset \mathbb{F}_{64}^\times, define the 14-bit column vector c(x) \in \{0,1\}^{14} by prepending two common bits (bit 0 = 1, bit 1 = 1) to the 12-bit binary representation of (x, x^3) \in \mathbb{F}_{64}^2:
c(x) = \text{0b11} \mid (x \ll 2) \mid (x^3 \ll 8)
Theorem 1 (Characteristic-2 Cubic Parabola Sidon Theorem)
The set S = \{(x, x^3) : x \in \mathbb{F}_{2^k}\} is an additive Sidon (B_2) set in \mathbb{F}_{2^k}^2. Consequently, all \binom{48}{2} = 1,128 integer pair sums \Sigma_2^{++} and all 2,256 ordered integer differences \Sigma_2^{+-} of C are strictly distinct in \mathbb{Z}^{14}.
Proof: Suppose (x + y, x^3 + y^3) = (u + v, u^3 + v^3) in \mathbb{F}_{2^k}^2 with x \neq y and u \neq v. Let s = x + y = u + v \neq 0. In characteristic 2, (x + y)^2 = x^2 + y^2, so:
x^3 + y^3 = (x + y)(x^2 + xy + y^2) = s(s^2 + xy) = s^3 + s \cdot xy
Equating s^3 + s \cdot xy = s^3 + s \cdot uv and dividing by s \neq 0 in the field \mathbb{F}_{2^k} yields xy = uv. Thus \{x, y\} and \{u, v\} have the same sum s and product p = xy, meaning both are the two roots of the quadratic polynomial T^2 + sT + p = 0 over \mathbb{F}_{2^k}[T]. Since a polynomial of degree 2 over a field has at most 2 roots, \{x, y\} = \{u, v\}. Now suppose two integer vectors satisfy c(x) + c(y) = c(u) + c(v) in \mathbb{Z}^{14}. Reducing each coordinate modulo 2 gives c(x) \oplus c(y) = c(u) \oplus c(v), which projects to (x+y, x^3+y^3) = (u+v, u^3+v^3) in \mathbb{F}_{64}^2, forcing \{x, y\} = \{u, v\}. Thus \vert{}\Sigma_2^{++}\vert{} = 1,128. Finally, for x \neq y and u \neq v, c(x) - c(y) = c(u) - c(v) \iff c(x) + c(v) = c(u) + c(y) in \mathbb{Z}^{14}. By the Sidon property, \{x, v\} = \{u, y\}. Since x \neq y, we cannot have x = y, so x = u and v = y. Thus \vert{}\Sigma_2^{+-}\vert{} = 2,256. \blacksquare
Theorem 2 (Automatic Minimum Distance \ge 2 and Opposite-Sign Pair Closure)
For every distinct x \neq y \in \mathbb{F}_{64}^\times, the Hamming distance satisfies \text{dist}(c(x), c(y)) \ge 2. Therefore, no opposite-sign pair syndrome c(x) - c(y) \in \Sigma_2^{+-} ever equals 0, a single column \pm c(z), or an axis vector \pm e_r.
Proof: Since x \neq y, the 6-bit difference x \oplus y \neq 0 has Hamming weight \text{wt}(x \oplus y) \ge 1.
* If \text{wt}(x \oplus y) \ge 2, then c(x) and c(y) already differ in at least 2 bit positions in rows 2\dots 7.
* If \text{wt}(x \oplus y) = 1, suppose x^3 = y^3. Then (x + y)^3 + xy(x + y) = 0 \implies (x + y)^2 = xy. However, in \mathbb{F}_{64} = \mathbb{F}_2[t]/(t^6+t+1), the map x \mapsto x^3 has kernel size \gcd(3, 63) = 3. Measure what is left over after an interaction; admit only what fits inside that leftover; otherwise

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- battery core
def battery(masks):
    """Exhaustive unit-amplitude battery. Definitions identical to the published
    battery.py shipped in the data drops (Models A / A+ / B as documented there);
    this is an independent reimplementation of those definitions."""
    r = max(m.bit_length() for m in masks)
    cols = [tuple((m >> k) & 1 for k in range(r)) for m in masks]
    def add(*vs): return tuple(sum(x) for x in zip(*vs))
    def neg(v): return tuple(-x for x in v)
    def sub(a, b): return tuple(x - y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    def scale(e, v): return tuple(e * x for x in v)
    zero = tuple([0] * r)
    rowsums = [sum(c[k] for c in cols) for k in range(r)]
    weights = [sum(c) for c in cols]
    mind = min(bin(masks[i] ^ masks[j]).count("1")
               for i in range(48) for j in range(i + 1, 48))
    units = [tuple(1 if j == k else 0 for j in range(r)) for k in range(r)]
    A = {zero}
    for c in cols: A.add(c); A.add(neg(c))
    for u in units: A.add(u); A.add(neg(u))
    Aplus = set(A)
    for e in (2, 3, -2, -3):
        for c in cols: Aplus.add(scale(e, c))
        for u in units: Aplus.add(scale(e, u))
    xor = {masks[i] ^ masks[j] for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(48), 2)}
    pp, pm, pair_syn = {}, {}, set()
    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(48), 2):
        s = add(cols[i], cols[j]); pp[s] = pp.get(s, 0) + 1; pair_syn.add(s)
    for i in range(48):
        for j in range(48):
            if i != j:
                s = sub(cols[i], cols[j]); pm[s] = pm.get(s, 0) + 1; pair_syn.add(s)
    B = A | pair_syn
    ppp, ppm = {}, {}
    acc = {"A": 0, "A+": 0, "B": 0}
    for i, j, k in itertools.combinations(range(48), 3):
        s = add(cols[i], cols[j], cols[k]); ppp[s] = ppp.get(s, 0) + 1
        if s in A: acc["A"] += 1
        if s in Aplus: acc["A+"] += 1
        if s in B: acc["B"] += 1
    for (i, j), k in itertools.product(itertools.combinations(range(48), 2), range(48)):
        if k != i and k != j:
            s = sub(add(cols[i], cols[j]), cols[k]); ppm[s] = ppm.get(s, 0) + 1
            if s in A: acc["A"] += 1
            if s in Aplus: acc["A+"] += 1
            if s in B: acc["B"] += 1
    trip_syn = set(ppp) | set(ppm)
    return {
        "r": r, "distinct": len(set(masks)), "nonzero": all(m != 0 for m in masks),
        "rowsums": rowsums, "total_bits": sum(rowsums),
        "wmin": min(weights), "wmax": max(weights), "mindist": mind,
        "common_bits": bin(masks[0] & masks[1] & masks[2] if False else
                           __import__("functools").reduce(int.__and__, masks)).count("1"),
        "xor_distinct": len(xor), "pp_distinct": len(pp), "pm_distinct": len(pm),
        "ppp_distinct": len(ppp), "ppm_distinct": len(ppm),
        "trip_distinct": len(trip_syn), "shared_ppp_ppm": len(set(ppp) & set(ppm)),
        "trip_eq_pair_distinct": len(trip_syn & pair_syn),
        "trip_eq_pp_distinct": len(trip_syn & set(pp)), "trip_eq_pm_distinct": len(trip_syn & set(pm)),
        "inter_pp_ppp": len(set(pp) & set(ppp)), "inter_pp_ppm": len(set(pp) & set(ppm)),
        "inter_pm_ppp": len(set(pm) & set(ppp)), "inter_pm_ppm": len(set(pm) & set(ppm)),
        "acc": acc, "_cols": cols, "_pair_syn": pair_syn,
    }

def codec_section(sec, masks, exp):
    print(f"\n--- {sec} (exhaustive battery, may take a minute) ---", flush=True)
    t0 = time.time()
    b = battery(masks)
    print(f"    battery ran in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s", flush=True)
    for key, label in [("distinct", "48 distinct masks"), ("rowsums", "row sums"),
                       ("total_bits", "total bits"), ("mindist", "min Hamming distance"),
                       ("xor_distinct", "XOR pair sums distinct /1128"),
                       ("pp_distinct", "integer ++ distinct /1128"),
                       ("pm_distinct", "ordered +- distinct /2256"),
                       ("ppp_distinct", "+++ distinct /17296"),
                       ("ppm_distinct", "++- distinct /51888"),
                       ("trip_distinct", "triple syndromes distinct /69184"),
                       ("shared_ppp_ppm", "syndromes shared by +++ and ++-"),
                       ("trip_eq_pair_distinct", "distinct triple syndromes equal to a pair syndrome")]:
        if key in exp: check(sec, label, b[key], exp[key])
    for mkey in ("A", "A+", "B"):
        if ("acc" + mkey) in exp: check(sec, f"weight-3 patterns accepted under Model {mkey}", b["acc"][mkey], exp["acc" + mkey])
    return b

# F64 quadruple pairing hits — predicate exactly as the v3 review's battery:
# for each 4-subset and each of its 3 pairings, s = (Va+Vb) - (Vc+Vd);
# axis (exactly one nonzero component) -> TAIL_EDIT; scalar multiple of a
# column -> REPAIRED (column-parallel). Sign orientation is irrelevant here.
print("--- MD S3.2 F64 quadruple pairing scan (583,740 syndromes) ---", flush=True)
_V = [tuple((m >> k) & 1 for k in range(14)) for m in F64]
def _is_axis(s): return sum(1 for x in s if x != 0) == 1
def _is_parallel(s):
    for col in _V:
        e = None; ok = True
        for k, ck in enumerate(col):
            if ck == 0:
                if s[k] != 0: ok = False; break
            else:
                if e is None:
                    e = s[k]
                    if e == 0: ok = False; break
                elif s[k] != e: ok = False; break
        if ok and e: return True
    return False

    # pairings: (w,x)|(y,z), (w,y)|(x,z), (w,z)|(x,y)
    for (a, b), (c, d) in (((w, x), (y, z)), ((w, y), (x, z)), ((w, z), (x, y))):
        s = tuple(aa + bb - cc - dd for aa, bb, cc, dd in zip(a, b, c, d))
        if _is_axis(s): _qa += 1
        elif _is_parallel(s): _qp += 1

# Any-amplitude silence check: no signed weight-<=3 syndrome is zero, axis-aligned,
# or parallel to a column. Sign classes +++ and ++- cover all patterns up to an
# overall sign, and all three properties are sign-invariant.
def _norm(v):
    g = 0
    for x in v: g = math.gcd(g, abs(x))
    if g == 0: return v
    w = tuple(x // g for x in v)
    for x in w:
        if x != 0:
            return tuple(-y for y in w) if x < 0 else w
    return w

def ktrace(n):
    """Backward trace from the paper: a(n) = K[n,n]; returns (a(n), terminal row, steps)."""
    i, j, steps = n, n, 0
    while j < 2 * i - 3:
        if j % 2 == 0: j = i - j // 2 - 1
        else: j = i + (j - 1) // 2
        i -= 1; steps += 1
    return i + j - 1, i, steps

1. Field
This disclosure relates to error-correcting codes for integer or real-valued data words. It covers
a binary parity check matrix whose columns are structured so that no pair fault and no
equal-magnitude triple fault can produce a syndrome that the decoder accepts as a correctable
single fault or as a parity-symbol edit. In the primary structural embodiment, the structure is an
integer Sidon set: all pairwise column sums are distinct as integer vectors. The preferred
construction takes the columns from the cubic parabola \{(x, x^3)\} in the finite field
\mathbb{F}_{64}, with two common bits set in every column. In a complementary
structural-and-confirmation embodiment, the matrix pairs a 7-row primary submatrix with its
7-row bitwise inverse mirror to enforce constant column weight 8, doubled pairwise Hamming
distances (D_{\min} = 2), and six linear mirror-conservation invariants across the syndrome,
optionally coupled with an 11-bit strictly convex triangular confirmation symbol.
In the unconfirmed Sidon matrix alone (Variant A), the protection covers all pairs and
equal-magnitude triples, and does not extend to all four-symbol faults: on the preferred
48-column cubic-parabola set, 81 of the 1,556,640 equal-magnitude (\pm 1) signed quadruple
faults have the sign pattern (+, +, -, -) and are accepted by Variant A as a parity-symbol edit
(TAIL_EDIT), while 0 are miscorrected as column repairs. When coupled with either the Variant
B confirmation check or the Dual-Mirror conservation check (s[k] + s[7+k] = s[0] = s[7]), 0 of the
1,556,640 equal-magnitude signed quadruple faults are accepted as TAIL_EDIT.

2. Background and Problem
A single-error-correcting code with columns drawn from odd binary words can repair a single
spike. However, some multi-symbol faults produce syndromes identical to a correctable single
fault, and the decoder then silently miscorrects. Two families of such faults are identified below:
●​ Opposite-sign aliases: A +1 spike on column a and a -1 spike on column b produce a
syndrome with a single nonzero row when the columns differ in exactly one bit position. In
the 7-row code with columns 3..97 (c_j = 2j+3 for j = 0..47), 124 of the 1,128 column pairs

a confirmation check, and each is misdiagnosed as a parity-symbol edit while the payload
holds two live spikes. These 124 pairs satisfy \vert{}a - b\vert{} = 2^k for k \in \{1, \dots, 6\}
(distributed 23, 23, 23, 23, 16, 16) and are exactly the 124 Hamming-distance-1 pairs.
●​ \pm 1 triple faults: Three spikes can reproduce the syndrome of a single column (door
triples, 7,140 ordered doors / 3,570 unordered doors over 944 door pairs in the 7-row
code, where c \lor d = a \lor b and c \land d = a \land b) or the syndrome of a single parity
row (single-row triples, 156). In the 7-row code, 7,296 of 69,184 equal-magnitude signed
triples alias under an unconfirmed or linearly-weighted (w_j = j+1) decoder.
A confirmation symbol u = \sum_j w_j v_j with strictly convex weights w_j = f(p_j) (such as
triangular weights f(p) = p(p+1)/2, requiring an 11-bit register for \max w_j = 1,176, or squared
weights f(p) = p^2, requiring a 12-bit register for \max w_j = 2,304) closes both families at the
decoder. This disclosure shows they can also be closed structurally, in the matrix alone: if all
pairwise column sums are distinct (a Sidon set), every column shares the same two common bit
positions, and the columns are pairwise at Hamming distance at least 2, then no pair fault and
no equal-magnitude triple fault can mimic a correctable single fault or a parity-symbol edit.
Section 7 describes further matrices, with fewer rows (r = 10..13) and with zero, one, or two

3. Code Construction
3.1 Matrix Dimensions
In the preferred embodiment, the code has N = 48 data positions, indexed j = 0..47. The parity
check matrix H has r = 14 rows. Column j is a 14-bit binary vector.

3.2 Two Common Bits
Bits 0 and 1 are set in every column. These are the common bits. Any fault pattern whose
integer syndrome is zero in row 0 or in row 1 cannot match e \cdot \text{column} for any nonzero
e, because every column has rows 0 and 1 set. A fault pattern whose syndrome is nonzero in
both rows 0 and 1 cannot match a single axis vector.

3.3 Cubic Parabola in \mathbb{F}_{64}
Let \mathbb{F}_{64} = \mathbb{F}_2[t]/(t^6+t+1), the finite field with 64 elements. Its additive
group is (\mathbb{Z}_2)^6, so each field element is 6 bits (bit i = coefficient of t^i). Consider the
cubic parabola S = \{(x, x^3) : x \in \mathbb{F}_{64}\}, a set of 64 points in \mathbb{F}_{64}^2,
each point 12 bits. Section 4 proves S is Sidon in the additive group: distinct unordered pairs
have distinct sums.
The cube map alone is not injective. Because \gcd(3, 63) = 3, the map x \mapsto x^3 is 3-to-1
on \mathbb{F}_{64}^*, and the 63 nonzero elements have only 21 distinct cubes (for example x
= 3, 13, and 14 have the same cube). The points (x, x^3) are nevertheless distinct, because
their x-coordinates are distinct. The Sidon property belongs to the pair (x, x^3), not to the cube
coordinate.

 3.4 Column Selection
From the 63 nonzero points of S, 48 are selected with pairwise Hamming distance at least 2 by
greedy selection: scan x = 1, 2, \dots, 63 (x read as the integer of its coefficient bits) and keep a
point if it is at distance \ge 2 from every point already kept, stopping at 48. Column j has bits 2..7
equal to x and bits 8..13 equal to x^3 for the j-th kept point; bits 0 and 1 are the common bits, so
\text{mask} = (\text{point} \ll 2) \mid 3 with \text{point} = x \mid (x^3 \ll 6). All 48 columns are
distinct.
Among the 63 nonzero points of S there are exactly 6 pairs at Hamming distance 1, and these 6
pairs share no point. The largest subset with pairwise distance at least 2 therefore has 63 - 6 =
57 points. The greedy scan, run without the stop at 48, reaches the same 57.

4. Sidon Theorem and Convexity Lemmas
4.1 Sidon Theorem (Characteristic 2)
Theorem 1. For q = 2^k, the set \{(x, x^3) : x \in \mathbb{F}_q\} is Sidon in the additive group
\mathbb{F}_q^2: equal pair sums imply equal pairs.
Proof. Suppose (x+y, x^3+y^3) = (u+v, u^3+v^3) with x \neq y and u \neq v. Put s = x+y = u+v. In
characteristic 2, x \neq y gives s \neq 0. Then x^3+y^3 = (x+y)(x^2+xy+y^2) = s(s^2+xy), using
x^2+y^2 = (x+y)^2 = s^2 in characteristic 2 (Freshman's dream). Similarly, u^3+v^3 = s(s^2+uv).
Hence s(s^2+xy) = s(s^2+uv), and since s \neq 0 in a field, xy = uv. Then \{x,y\} and \{u,v\} are
both root-sets of t^2+st+xy = 0, which has at most two roots; thus \{x,y\} = \{u,v\} as multisets.
\blacksquare
Corollary. The 1,128 pairwise sums of the 48 selected columns, taken as integer vectors
(entries 0, 1, 2), are all distinct. Proof: Equal integer-vector sums reduce mod 2 to equal XOR
sums; the common bits contribute the same value to every sum; Theorem 1 then forces the
pairs equal, a contradiction. The same holds for any subset of S. Equivalently, no triple (+,+,-) of
columns can reproduce a fourth column: \text{col}[i] + \text{col}[j] - \text{col}[k] = \text{col}[m]
would require \text{col}[i] + \text{col}[j] = \text{col}[k] + \text{col}[m] as integer vectors,
contradicting distinctness. \blacksquare
Necessity. Integer Sidon is also necessary, for every matrix whatever its common bits: if
\text{col}[a] + \text{col}[b] = \text{col}[c] + \text{col}[d] for four distinct columns, the
equal-magnitude triple (+a, +b, -c) has syndrome \text{col}[d] and is repaired at the wrong
position. Pairwise distance at least 2 is likewise necessary for the decoder of Variant A (Section
5.2): a distance-1 pair gives an opposite-sign syndrome with a single nonzero row.

4.2 Strictly Convex Confirmation Lemmas (for Variant B and
Dual-Mirror Codes)
Lemma 1 (Strict Convexity). Let f be strictly convex on the integers, and let a + b = c + d with
\{a, b\} \neq \{c, d\}. Then the pair that is more spread out, with the larger |x - y|, has the strictly
larger value of f(x) + f(y). In particular, f(a) + f(b) \neq f(c) + f(d).
Proof. Write s = a + b = c + d and write each pair as (s/2 - \delta, s/2 + \delta) with \delta = |x y|/2 \ge 0. Define g(\delta) = f(s/2 - \delta) + f(s/2 + \delta). For 0 \le \delta_1 < \delta_2, write s/2
+ \delta_1 = t(s/2 + \delta_2) + (1-t)(s/2 - \delta_2) and s/2 - \delta_1 = (1-t)(s/2 + \delta_2) +
t(s/2 - \delta_2) with t = (\delta_1 + \delta_2)/(2\delta_2) \in (1/2, 1). Strict convexity gives f(s/2 +
\delta_1) < t f(s/2 + \delta_2) + (1-t) f(s/2 - \delta_2) and f(s/2 - \delta_1) < (1-t) f(s/2 + \delta_2)
+ t f(s/2 - \delta_2). Adding the two inequalities yields g(\delta_1) < g(\delta_2). Since \{a, b\}

 \neq \{c, d\}, the two pairs have different \delta, and the f-sums differ strictly. \blacksquare
Lemma 2 (Single-Row Relation). For triangular weights f(p) = p(p+1)/2, f(a) + f(b) - f(a+b) =
-ab. For squared weights f(p) = p^2, it is -2ab. In both cases the value is nonzero for a, b \ge 1.
Proof. Expand directly: [a(a+1) + b(b+1) - (a+b)(a+b+1)]/2 = -ab, and a^2 + b^2 - (a+b)^2 = -2ab.
For a, b \ge 1, -ab \le -1 < 0 and -2ab \le -2 < 0. \blacksquare

5. Refusal of Pair, Triple, and Quadruple Faults
5.1 Case Analysis (Two-Common-Bit Sidon Matrix)
The errors considered here are pairs and triples whose nonzero entries all have the same
magnitude m, with either sign. Because the decoder's decision does not change when the
syndrome is multiplied by a nonzero scalar, m = 1 may be assumed. "Match" below means the
syndrome equals e \cdot \text{col}(m) or e \cdot e_k for some nonzero scalar e (a scaled column
or a scaled axis vector), or is zero. These are the syndromes the decoder does not refuse:
●​ Pair (+,+) on columns a \neq b: Rows 0 and 1 carry 1+1 = 2, so the syndrome is neither
zero nor an axis vector. A match e \cdot \text{col}(m) would need every nonzero row equal
to 2, i.e., \text{col}(a) = \text{col}(b), which is excluded. Refused.
●​ Pair (+,-): Rows 0 and 1 are 1-1 = 0, so no column matches. The support is the
symmetric difference of the two columns, which has at least 2 rows by the distance-\ge 2
selection, so the syndrome is neither zero nor an axis vector. Refused.
●​ Triple (+,+,+): Rows 0 and 1 carry 3, so not zero and not an axis. A match needs e = 3
and every nonzero row equal to 3, i.e., three identical columns. Impossible / Refused.
●​ Triple (+,+,-) \to e \cdot \text{column}: Row 0 is 1+1-1 = 1, so e = 1 (this also covers the
-\text{column} case since e = -1 is impossible when row 0 is +1). Then \text{col}[i] +
\text{col}[j] - \text{col}[k] = \text{col}[m] requires a repeated pair sum \text{col}[i] +
\text{col}[j] = \text{col}[k] + \text{col}[m], which the Sidon Corollary forbids. Refused.
●​ Triple (+,+,-) \to e \cdot e_0: Row 1 is 1 \neq 0. Impossible / Refused. (For parabola
columns this case is excluded even with a single common bit; see Section 7.2.)
●​ Triple (+,+,-) \to e \cdot e_m, m > 0: Row 0 is 1 \neq 0. Impossible / Refused.
●​ Triple (+,+,-) \to \text{zero}: Row 0 is 1 \neq 0. Impossible / Refused.
●​ Patterns (+,-,-) and (-,-,-): Negatives of the above; refused by symmetry.

5.2 Proof of Total Single-Row (TAIL_EDIT) Immunity under Dual-Mirror
Conservation
In the 14-row Dual-Mirror matrix H_{\text{dual}} (Section 3.6), let \mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^{48}
be any payload fault vector (including any equal-magnitude signed quadruple fault).
1.​ Because Row 0 and Row 7 are all-ones rows and H[7+k, j] = 1 - H[k, j] for k = 1..6, the
syndrome satisfies s[0] = s[7] = \sum_j e_j and s[k] + s[7+k] = \sum_j e_j = s[0] for all k =
1..6.
2.​ If \mathbf{s} is supported on a single row r, it cannot be r = 0 or r = 7 because s[0] = s[7].
3.​ If r \in \{1..6\} \cup \{8..13\}, then s[0] = s[7] = 0, which forces s[7+k] = -s[k] for every k =
1..6. Any nonzero syndrome entry in row k forces an equal-and-opposite nonzero entry in
row 7+k, so the syndrome support size is at least 2 (specifically, an even integer 2w \ge
2).
4.​ Therefore, zero payload faults of any weight (pairs, triples, quadruples, or higher)

 can ever produce a single-row syndrome (TAIL_EDIT) in H_{\text{dual}}.

5.3 Decoder Variants
The decoder is a repair-or-refuse decoder working on the signed integer or real syndrome s = H
\cdot v - t, with relative tolerance in floating-point implementations. In all variants, it repairs
position j only when the support of s equals the support of column j and all nonzero entries of s
share one value e (s = e \cdot \text{col}(j)), and it refuses every syndrome that is not zero, not
such a column match, and not a single-row syndrome.
●​ Variant A (no confirmation symbol; reference: level100_v4.py, classify): A syndrome
with exactly one nonzero row, of any row and any nonzero value, is classed as
TAIL_EDIT: an edit of the corresponding check (parity) symbol, returning the payload
unchanged. It is not refused. (The reference code labels this outcome "axis".) This is the
preferred embodiment for the Sidon matrix and the decoder used for the figures in
Sections 6 and 7.
●​ Variant B (confirmed or unconfirmed; reference: canon codec.py, Codec.decode): A
single-row syndrome is accepted as TAIL_EDIT only when a confirmation symbol u =
\sum_j w_j v_j is stored and the confirmation residual q = \sum_j w_j v_j - u is zero; in that
confirmed form a repair at position j additionally requires q = e \cdot w_j, and a zero
syndrome outputs CLEAN when q = 0 or CONFIRMATION_EDIT when q \neq 0.
Otherwise the single-row syndrome is refused. In the unconfirmed form of Variant B (no
u), every single-row syndrome is refused, so pure parity-symbol edits are refused rather
than classed as TAIL_EDIT.
Variant B accepts a subset of what Variant A accepts, so every fault refused under Variant A is
also refused under Variant B. Every refusal is logged with its syndrome, residual, and reason.

7. Reduced Row Counts and Mathematical Bounds
7.1 Lower Bounds (Incorporating Errata 02: E4a, E4b, E4c)
Integer Sidon (Section 4) is equivalent to all N(N-1) ordered differences \text{col}[a] - \text{col}[b]
being distinct. With k rows that are not common, these differences are nonzero vectors in \{-1, 0,
1\}^k, and by the distance-\ge 2 condition none has a single nonzero entry. Counting differences
up to sign gives:
\frac{N(N-1)}{2} \le \frac{3^k - 1 - 2k}{2}
For k = 7, (3^7 - 1)/2 = 1,093 difference classes, and 1,086 once the 14 single-entry classes are
removed by distance \ge 2; both are below the 1,128 pairs of a 48-column code. For k = 8 the
difference bound is 3,272 and excludes nothing. Hence, for N = 48:
●​ Any matrix, with or without common bits: r \le 7 is impossible (proved).
●​ One common bit: r \ge 9.
●​ Two common bits: r \le 9 is impossible (proved). At r = 10 a sharper argument limits the
free part (8 rows) to at most 37 columns, so 48 columns are impossible. This combines
Delsarte's linear-programming inequalities (using the Krawtchouk polynomial sum g(w) =
45, 13, 13, -3, -3, -3, -3, 13, 13 for w = 0..8, which gives certificate constant +5/4 at N = 37
and -43 at N = 38) with distance caps that follow from distinct integer pair sums
(\binom{8}{w}\min(2^{8-w}, 2^{w-1})): at most 56 pairs at distance 2, 16 at distance 7, and
1 at distance 8 (from the complement argument). Subsets inherit the refusal conditions,
so every N \ge 38 is also excluded.
The difference-counting step uses differences because pair sums alone do not give a bound at k
= 7: sums of two distinct 0/1 vectors on 7 rows can take 3^7 - 2^7 = 2,059 values, more than
1,128.
Whether a general matrix with r = 8 or r = 9 rows can carry 48 columns is open (the largest
general set found at r = 9 has 39 columns, per RESULTS.md / long_r9_m0_s11.txt and s12.txt).

 Whether a two-common-bit matrix with r = 11 rows can carry 48 columns is open. The largest
such set found has 45 columns (RESULTS.md / long_r11_m1_s11.txt), and a
linear-programming certificate limits the free part (9 rows) to at most 58.
For comparison, bounds that hold at every n for integer-Sidon subsets of \{0,1\}^n (pair sums
distinct, no distance condition) are N \le 65, 110, 185, and 315 for n = 8, 9, 10, and 11. These
follow from Lindström's inequality |A| < M^{1/2} + M^{1/4} + 1 for Sidon sets in [1, M], applied
through the base-3 embedding x \mapsto \sum x_i 3^{i-1} + 1 with M = (3^n + 1)/2.
Ordered-difference counting gives the weaker N \le 81, 140, 243, and 421. The published
asymptotic bounds for binary B_2 sequences (2^{0.6n} and 2^{0.5753n} for large n) state no
explicit form at finite n and do not apply at n = 8 to 11. These bounds ignore the distance-\ge 2
condition, so they apply a fortiori to the sets of this disclosure. None of them excludes 48.

This 13-row matrix refuses all 2,256 pairs and all 69,184 equal-magnitude triples, both by

9. Alternative Embodiments
●​ Other Sidon sets: Any set of N binary vectors with all pairwise integer-vector sums
distinct and pairwise Hamming distance at least 2, combined with two common bits, may
replace the cubic-parabola selection.

where every pair and every equal-magnitude signed triple of columns meets the refusal
conditions of Claim 8, for example the 10- to 13-row sets of Section 7.
●​ Other fields and larger codes: The cubic parabola \{(x, x^3)\} is Sidon over
\mathbb{F}_q for any q = 2^k; larger fields give larger column pools. For q = 64, the
maximum distance-\ge 2 subset of nonzero parabola points has size N = 57 (verified
exhaustively).

be used; in Variant B, the confirmation weights may be any strictly convex function f(p_j)
such as the 11-bit triangular weights w_j = (j+1)(j+2)/2 or 12-bit squared weights w_j =
(j+1)^2, or any pairwise-distinct nonzero weights when paired with a Sidon matrix.
●​ Other odd windows (7-row and Dual-Mirror families): In the 7-row confirmation code,
the window 3..97 gives 7,140 doors, while the contiguous odd windows starting at 1, 17,
and 33 (1..95, 17..111, 33..127) give 7,440 doors; any of these windows may be used.

## 1. The doctrine

The Ultimate Edition is not a prettier picture of the work. It is the work, at full visual power, with nothing on screen that is not true.

- **Every figure is a flex.** Every number, count, period, angle, and density that appears in any piece is a measured figure from the verified record, shown at maximum presence — never decoration, never filler.
- **Every aesthetic is a measurement.** Wire counts are Hamming counts. Node sizes are degrees. Motion periods are the measured animation periods. Color is data class. If a visual element cannot name the figure it carries, it does not ship.
- **Mind-blowing is a spec, not a mood.** The chrome wire-tunnel inheritance (maximum wires, calligraphy vortex, the Oct 10 directive: *everything learned, packed in*) fused with the GENESIS lattice — the tunnel is built out of the data, and the data is the flex.
- **The anti-flex list is constitutional** (from the Oct 14 masterpiece correction): no invented layouts — node positions come from `touchdesigner_nodes.csv` or they do not appear; no borrowed figures (the 162/141 error never recurs); DMX live, never disabled for looks; metrics files never zero-byte; an art claim and a measured claim are never blurred.

## 2. The suite — three pieces, one math

**Piece I — THE RIG (the moving masterpiece).** The TouchDesigner build, ultimate spec: the canonical GENESIS data rendered through the wire-tunnel — the camera flies the tunnel while the 48-node lattice turns inside it, every strand a real edge. Post stack as proven on masterpiece v2 (bloom, feedback, GLSL), 60 fps floor as a hard gate, DMX driving the 9 universes live.

**Piece II — THE TUNNEL PLATES (the stills).** Print-scale plates (3200×1800 minimum, 4K master) in the chrome wire-tunnel / calligraphy-vortex language: one plate per domain face of the same math — the lattice plate, the closed-set plate, the spectral plate, the refusal plate — each plate's geometry generated from its own domain's measured figures, each carrying its flex ledger as inscription.

**Piece III — THE FLEX LEDGER (the inscription system).** Every piece carries its figures printed into the work itself, the way masterpiece v1 carried its count lines — but now every line is a verified figure with its source named: what was measured, where, and what remains open. The ledger is part of the art. A viewer who reads nothing else reads the truth.

Electronic Devices

In spring 2024, the EPS Board of Education approved updates to student handbooks to align expectations for the use of cell phones and personal electronic devices across EPS schools at all levels and further protect instructional time by reducing the number of outside distractions.  The updates were approved in alignment with the EPS Strategic Plan goal focusing on “the mental health and overall well-being of students and staff”, and the recently released U.S. Surgeon General advisory stating the negative impacts of social media on teens’ mental health.

The updated cell phone expectations, as shown below and reflected in all student handbooks, will be implemented for the 2024-25 school year for EPS buildings at all levels. 

ELEMENTARY
Elementary students will keep personal electronic devices (including cell phones, smart watches, earbuds, etc.) powered off and placed in backpacks during the school day.  It is the recommendation of the school district that devices be left at home as the school is not responsible for devices brought to school.  If parents/guardians need to communicate with their child during the school day, they should contact the school office and a message will be shared with the student. Students who need electronic devices to monitor health conditions will continue to follow their individualized plans.

Handbook Verbiage (found on page 8 of Elementary Student Handbook)
Cellular phones and devices, including cellular watches, are strongly discouraged at school to minimize distractions to the learning environment. The use of cellular devices is not permitted throughout the day. Students must keep the devices powered off in their backpacks or the office area, and they are to be used only after dismissal at the end of the day. If this procedure is not followed, the device will be kept in the office area and a parent/guardian may collect the device from the office.
